title: Why Janine Allis Tested Boost Juice in Adelaide, Not Melbourne
dek: In 2000 a Melbourne mother on maternity leave opened her first juice bar in a smaller city, where mistakes would cost less and be seen by fewer.

story.event: Opening the first Boost Juice Bar in Adelaide rather than her home city
story.summary: After seeing a smoothie bar in the United States in 1999 and a failed juice-bar partnership in Melbourne, Janine Allis, then on maternity leave, opened the first Boost Juice Bar on King William Street, Adelaide, in 2000, choosing a smaller market for lower risk and room to learn. Two more shops opened that year, the business moved into franchising as imitators appeared, and by October 2004 it had more than 140 stores.
paragraphs: In September 1999 Janine Allis, a Melbourne marketing executive who had worked for Village Roadshow, came across a smoothie bar on a trip to the United States. She liked the concept, though not, she said later, the American version of it. Australia, as she saw it, had no healthy drink you could simply grab on the way somewhere, and she was frustrated at how hard it was to find healthy takeaway food for her children.

Her first attempt did not last. A juice bar she opened with partners in Chapel Street, Prahran, ended when the partnership failed. She tried again while on maternity leave from a publicity job at United International Pictures, with a newborn, a two-year-old and an eight-year-old at home. The plan, she later admitted, was "a little business, work my own hours, probably part-time, be a mum".

The decision that shaped Boost was where to begin. Allis lived in Melbourne, but she and her husband Jeff chose Adelaide, judging that a smaller market carried less financial risk. In 2003 she said it let them get going "without many prying eyes" and gave them "the time to learn from our mistakes". Before committing to a site, Jeff asked his father to sit outside it and count passers-by, noting whether they were men or women and roughly how old. The first Boost Juice Bar opened on King William Street in 2000; the business itself was started in her garage.

Her own accounts of the next months differ. In 2009 she said the distance meant she worked on the business rather than in it, with a good manager on the shop floor; a Boost web page quoted in 2012 had her flying over to run the store and scrub its floors. Either way, the part-time plan did not survive. She recalled 80-hour weeks and work at two in the morning. Two more shops opened that year, imitators followed, and Boost moved early into franchising. By October 2004 it had more than 140 stores, and she was named Telstra Australian Business Woman of the Year.

quote.text: if the American artist will study with hope and love the precise thing to be done by him, considering the climate, the soil, the length of the day, the wants of the people, the habit and form of the government, he will create a house in which all these will find themselves fitted
quote.source_title: Essays — First Series, Project Gutenberg eBook #2944
quote.connection: Emerson urged American builders to stop copying European models and design for their own climate and people. Allis made the journey the other way, taking an American idea home and reshaping it, by her account, for Australian customers, then testing it where it could be fitted quietly.

reflection: Allis chose a place where her first mistakes would cost less and be seen by fewer people. That is not timidity. It is a way of buying time to learn, and it is open to almost anyone starting something new.

The other half of her story is the plan that did not survive: a small, part-time business that became eighty-hour weeks with three children at home. You may know that pull already. It helps to decide, before the work decides for you, which hours belong to your family and your rest, and to tell someone who will hold you to it.
invitation: Choose one idea you have been reluctant to show anyone, and name the smallest, most forgiving place where you could try it first this week.

research_notes: The US trip: The Age (2003) dates it to September 1999, while the SMH (2009) says the Allises found the idea on a US trip 'in the mid-'90s'; the story uses the earlier-published, more precise date. Her role at the first store: in the SMH (2009) she says that because Adelaide was far from home she worked 'ON the business' and hired a manager for the floor, while SmartCompany (2012) quotes her, from the Boost website, saying she flew to Adelaide, ran the store and scrubbed the floors; the story reports both. Store numbers: The Age (October 2004) says more than 140 stores, the SMH (2009) says 150 shops had opened by 2004 and the SMH (December 2004) gives 140 stores in Australia and New Zealand; the story uses 'more than 140 by October 2004'. Her employer: the SMH says a PR job at United International Pictures, The Age (2004) a marketing role at United Pictures and Village Roadshow; the story names United International Pictures for the maternity leave and Village Roadshow for her earlier career. Funding is given as bootstrapped: profiles (not loadable here) say friends helped fund the first store, and The Age (2003) reports the first outside shareholder, Flight Centre co-founder Geoff Harris, came in during 2002. The SMH and Age pages are marked as paywalled but serve the full text. Boost's own history page (boostjuice.com.au/about) now returns 404, so its wording is taken from SmartCompany's quotation. Emerson's passage urges American artists to design for American conditions rather than copy Europe; it is applied by analogy to adapting an American concept for Australia.
